newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl offer of jobs summit gets cool response.
newsitem.headline: Kohl offer of jobs summit gets cool response.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's offer on Thursday to chair a jobs summit to fight soaring unemployment drew a cool response from Germany's top trade union chief after similar talks collapsed in acrimony last year.

Speaking after new data showed that December unemployment hit a post-war record of 4.16 million, seasonally adjusted, Kohl said his goal of halving dole queues by the year 2000 would be difficult -- but not impossible -- to achieve.
"Fighting unemployment remains the most important domestic policy challenge," Kohl told a news conference. "Current levels of over 4.1 million jobless are completely unacceptable."
Kohl's tentative offer to host new round table policy talks got the cold shoulder from unions who quit the "alliance for jobs" last year in disgust at government austerity policies.
Dieter Schulte, chairman of the German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB), said talks were unlikely because Bonn "lacked the courage" to admit that its policies were swelling dole queues.
The 14-year-old Kohl government's belt-tightening is aimed at ensuring Bonn meets the Maastricht treaty's borrowing limits to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Kohl, who wants the euro single currency to be launched on time in 1999, said he opposed a national referendum on EMU as it would be illegal under Germany's post-war constitution.
But he said he was sure of winning over a sceptical German public to the cause of monetary union in the end.
"I am confident that when...people have all the information we will get a clear majority of the population for the euro," the Chancellor.
Attacking Kohl on the economy, the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said his government offered "no ideas and vague promises" on overcoming the worst jobs crisis since the 1930s.
"Mass unemployment threatens social stability in Germany," SPD economics spokesman Ernst Schwanhold said.

Headline December jobless figures, not seasonally adjusted, surged to 4.15 million, or 10.8 percent of the workforce, and could hit 4.5 million this winter, Federal Labour Office head Bernhard Jagoda said.

Kohl said immigration from eastern Europe after the fall of the Berlin Wall had been one cause of rising unemployment. But he said he could not fathom why firms were still shedding staff while their remaining workers racked up record overtime.
Cutting back overtime -- one aspect of the defunct jobs alliance which unions say employers reneged on -- could create hundreds of thousands of new jobs, he said.
Despite record unemployment, Kohl was still upbeat on the outlook for the German economy. "Chances for recovery rest on a solid basis," he said. "Creating jobs is possible."
Underpinning prospects for economic recovery were low interest rates, price stability, a positive global outlook, a weaker mark and moderate wage settlements.
Kohl also dismissed as unfounded a pessimistic forecast of two percent growth this year by the DIW research institute -- one of a panel of six whose forecasts underpin budget policy.
He said he still backed the six institutes' forecast from last autumn of 2.5 percent growth.

Preliminary data showed on Thursday that the economy grew a sluggish 1.4 percent in 1996, while the budget deficit jumped to 3.9 percent of GDP -- above the Maastricht ceiling of three percent, the Federal Statistics Office said.
Kohl's coalition is in the home stretch of arduous talks on drafting a common strategy to streamline Germany's tax system and help keep down state borrowing in the long term.

He said a coalition working group would complete its work this month on a strategy to cut income taxes and scrap a range of tax breaks from 1999. But consultations over thrashing out final legislation would continue all year, he added.
